## Chapter 1: From Tough Coaches, Tough Parents, and Tough Guys to Finding Real Inner Strength

**The Old Model of Toughness**

College students described toughness as: hard-nosed, gritty, playing through pain, stoic, showing no signs of distress, persevering. Among 160 elite athletes, perseverance came out on top. The traditional image is a football player popping a dislocated shoulder back in, or Craig MacTavish (last NHL player without a helmet, retired 1997).

Bobby Knight won over 900 games (third most all-time), three NCAA championships, and a perfect 1976 season. He defined toughness as "Being able to overcome obstacles. You can't feel sorry for yourself." His methods included: tampons hung in lockers of players he thought "soft," cussing out players, accusations of taping pictures of women's genitalia in players' rooms, a 1991 tirade ("This is absolute fucking bullshit..."), bringing toilet paper with shit to show players what he thought of them, and choking a player at practice. All in the name of creating Knight's version of toughness, founded on showing no weakness, bulldozing through obstacles, and using fear to establish authority.

**Tough Parenting**

Developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind (1960s) classified parenting styles by two factors: responsiveness (attuned, supportive, fostering individuality) and demandingness (expectations, control, discipline).

- **Permissive**: low demandingness, high responsiveness (too soft)
- **Authoritarian**: high demandingness, low responsiveness (too hard) – relies on fear, threats, punishment; typical refrain: "You need to do (this) because I said so." In one study of over 1,000 parents, only 31% of authoritarian parents said they should "love their child unconditionally."
- **Authoritative**: high demandingness AND high responsiveness ("just right" Goldilocks fit)

In one study, 81% of Americans thought parents were too soft on their children. The problem arises when demandingness far outweighs support.

**Callousness vs. Real Toughness**

"Callous" means to harden, make insensitive, develop thick skin. We romanticize the Karate Kid narrative. In youth sports, Mark Hyman (Until It Hurts) found frequent throwing up after workouts and insult-laden tirades. Parent justification: "The stern approach is necessary for children to get in touch with their inner lacrosse warrior."

Toughness has been tied to masculinity and machismo: "man up," "stop being a pussy," "There's no crying in baseball!" (A League of Their Own). The image is more The Rock or Vin Diesel than a small female of similar prowess. Women, who research shows quietly handle pain better than men, may have had the correct definition all along.

**Consequences of the Callous View**

On May 29, 2018, University of Maryland football player Jordan McNair (19) showed signs of profound fatigue during ten 110-yard sprints. Coaches yelled to "get him the [expletive] up" and "drag his [expletive] across the field." It took trainers 34 minutes to get him off the field, another 28 minutes to call 911. McNair died two weeks later from heatstroke.

Rhabdomyolysis (rhabdo) – damaged muscle products leaking into bloodstream – has become more common from extreme workouts designed to "test" athletes, not improve fitness. Professor B. David Ridpath (Ohio University): "Taking a cue from a head coach with a desire to either toughen up the current players or weed out a few... the strength coach often will 'condition' these players with a vengeance."

Authoritarian parenting leads to lower independence, more aggressive behavior, higher likelihood of substance abuse and risky behaviors. In sport, it's linked to lower grit, increased emotional exhaustion, burnout, and fear of failure. In one study of over 1,200 parents, authoritarian parenting was linked to much higher rates of child misbehavior. In the Israeli military, those from authoritarian environments coped worse with military challenges.

One young athlete: "Coaches use exercise as punishment because they want you to become stronger... I need to work harder because I don't want to be punished." He wanted to avoid punishment, not get better.

**Redefining Toughness**

Fake toughness is: control- and power-driven, developed through fear, fueled by insecurity, based on appearance over substance.

Real toughness: experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action. It's navigating discomfort to make the best decision you can.

Pete Carroll (only one of three coaches to win both NCAA championship and Super Bowl) believes toughness comes from inner drive, embracing challenges, perseverance and passion. He uses "always compete" practices but recognizes his job is to give players skills to handle adversity: "Teaching guys how to feel confident enough to believe in what they've been prepared to do." Other successful coaches with similar approaches: Don Shula, Bill Walsh, Tony Dungy (NFL); John Wooden, Dean Smith, Brad Stevens, Mike D'Antoni (basketball). D'Antoni told Magness: "We keep it positive here." Ken Reed (Ego vs. Soul in Sports): "For every Lombardi or Bobby Knight you give me, I can give you an equally successful—if not more successful—humanistic coach."

2008 research from Eastern Washington on nearly 200 basketball players: "The 'keys' to promoting mental toughness do not lie in this autocratic, authoritarian, or oppressive style. It appears to lie... with the coach's ability to produce an environment, which emphasizes trust and inclusion, humility, and service."

**Magness's Personal Story**

Magness was racing the Don Bowden Mile (Bowden was first American to break 4-minute mile in 1957). At 900 meters into the 1,609-meter race, he experienced a strange high-pitched gasp. His inner voice: "I can't breathe. What the hell!? I can't breathe!" He collapsed. Diagnosis: paradoxical vocal cord dysfunction (VCD) – vocal cords shut when they should open, blocking inhalation. The American Thoracic Society cites "strong emotions" and stress as triggers. Magness had to learn to relax and keep his breathing, neck, and mind steady at the exact moment discomfort was highest.

**The Four Pillars of Real Toughness**
1. Ditch the Facade, Embrace Reality
2. Listen to Your Body
3. Respond Instead of React
4. Transcend Discomfort

## Chapter 10: Build the Foundation to Do Hard Things

**Cultlike Environments vs. Healthy Teams**

Julie, a college freshman, was told competitors were "enemies." Her coach posted a ranking list on her office door, made snide remarks about Julie's weight, asked about her personal life, and said "Sex makes you gain weight." The coach said "It's us against the world." Julie reflects: "It's almost like we were in a cult."

Research identifies four key elements controlling leaders use to create dependence: controlling use of rewards, negative conditional regard, intimidation and isolation, excessive personal control.

**The Myth of External Motivation**

A meta-analysis covering over 120 years found less than 2% overlap between salary and job satisfaction. A Gallup study of over 1.4 million employees found no relationship between employee engagement and level of pay. People motivated by inner drive are three times more engaged than those motivated by external factors.

In a study of over 100 British athletes, inner drive led to better persistence, seeing challenges instead of threats, and using positive coping strategies. Externally motivated individuals were more likely to disengage and see the endeavor as a threat.

**Reengagement**

Analysis of nearly 100 years of deaths on Everest: of climbers who made it to the death zone (over 8,000 meters), only 10% died going up, while 73% died coming down. Tough individuals can reengage – shift goals when persistence is unwise. Psychologists call this autonomous motivation.

**Self-Determination Theory (SDT)**

Edward Deci and Richard Ryan: three basic psychological needs – autonomy (feeling in control), competence (making progress), relatedness (belonging). Needs satisfaction is linked to better health, well-being, and performance.

John Mahoney's PhD dissertation on over 200 cross-country runners and rowers: satisfying the three basic needs was related to toughness and improved racing times. The social environment (primarily the coach) played a large role. Toughness resulted from "coaching behaviors that promote psychological needs satisfaction."

**Abusive Leadership**

Erica Carleton and Mark Beauchamp studied 57 NBA head coaches (2000-2006). Players under coaches using abusive leadership (ridicule, blame) saw a clear drop in player efficiency score. The effect stretched to the player's entire career trajectory. Players also had more technical fouls (aggression) throughout their careers. Paper title: "Scarred for the Rest of My Career? Career-Long Effects of Abusive Leadership on Professional Athlete Aggression and Task Performance."

Sports psychologist Laura Healy: "When athletes perceive their coaches to be more autonomy supportive, they report greater satisfaction of their basic psychological needs, and consequently strive for their goals with higher autonomous motives."

**Support, Not Thwart**

Steve Kerr (Golden State Warriors coach, 44-13 record in February 2018, defending champions) turned over coaching duties to players Andre Iguodala and Draymond Green for a game. Kerr: "It's the players' team... They determine their own fate." The Warriors won 129-83.

Research from Eastern Washington University on 64 NCAA track teams: athletes under servant (supportive) coaches scored higher on mental toughness and ran faster than those under power (thwarting) coaches. In a study of over 1,000 office workers, the strongest predictor of dealing with demanding work was feeling respected and valued by managers.

**Progress and Psychological Safety**

Google's two-year study on team performance: the top characteristic of good teams was psychological safety – "Can we take risks on this team without feeling insecure or embarrassed?"

**Belonging**

Michael Kraus, Cassey Huang, and Dacher Keltner (2010) tracked nearly 300 NBA players' behaviors during the 2008-2009 season. Teams with more fist bumps, high fives, and positive interactions had better performance. The key wasn't the acts themselves but what they represented: trust and belonging.

Psychologist Scott Barry Kaufman: "When one feels belonging, one feels accepted and seen, and when one is deprived of belonging, one feels rejected and invisible." The brain interprets rejection similarly to physical pain.

The calm-and-connect system releases opioids (dampening cortisol) and oxytocin (turning down the amygdala alarm system). Oxytocin only leads to increased connection when the person is deemed trustworthy.

Gregg Popovich (San Antonio Spurs coach) uses three-hour team meals with expertly chosen wine and food. Players report being friends with every teammate. Research on soldiers in the Iraq War: the deep emotional bond between soldiers came out on top as motivation. The key was "conversation during noncombat time—the hours of nothingness, the shared boredom—where bonds of trust, friendships, and group identity are built."

Dan Coyle (The Culture Code) describes the "vulnerability loop": we don't need trust before vulnerability; we need vulnerability to build trust.

**Maslow's Hierarchy**

Abraham Maslow's famous pyramid was created by someone else. In his 1970 journal, Maslow wrote self-actualization was "too sloppy & too easily criticizable." His final rendering placed self-transcendence at the highest rung. Maslow wrote that society pushes us against it as "most industrialists will carefully conceal their idealism... under a mask of toughness."

## Chapter 11: Find Meaning in Discomfort

**Viktor Frankl**

A 41-year-old MD/PhD candidate delivered five Saturday lectures on "Suicide-forced annihilation, the world of the mentally ill, sexual education" and the "Experimentum Crucis." He declared happiness "should not, must not, and can never be a goal, but only an outcome." Three ways to fulfillment: (1) doing/creating, (2) experiencing (nature, love, art), (3) suffering. "True suffering of an authentic fate is an achievement, and, indeed, is the highest possible achievement."

Frankl had previously given this lecture mentally while in a concentration camp with 280 others, split into rows of 5, discussing the soup for dinner. He visualized being in the lecture hall and began his lecture "The Psychology of the Concentration Camp."

**The Will to Continue**

Performance = Actual effort / Expected Effort × Drive. Drive determines how close to zero we can push. The body has a safety mechanism – like a car's gas gauge that shows zero before the tank is actually empty. The brain weighs risk vs. reward to set the governor.

**Frankl's Experience**

Frankl entered Theresienstadt in 1942 with a manuscript sewn into his jacket (confiscated). He lost his mother, father, and wife. He observed phases: shock ("Everyone in this situation flirts... with the idea of running into the wire"), then apathy (death met with "Hmm"). Survivors Lou and Esther reported feeling "numb and living a day at a time... First, you want to die. Then you want to survive."

Frankl: "Despite the cruelty visited on prisoners by the guards... there was one part of their lives that remained free: their own minds." Freedom to choose how you experienced suffering. Those who did not survive were not the weakest but among the strongest. Frankl's meaning: to return to loved ones and finish his life's work. "I am convinced that I owe my survival, among other things, to my resolve to reconstruct that lost manuscript."

**Post-Traumatic Growth (PTG)**

Studies on former POWs from the Vietnam War: the longer a POW spent in captivity, the more physical injuries, the higher the growth. Psychiatrist Adriana Feder (Mount Sinai): "Severe trauma triggers a search for meaning and a fundamental reconfiguration of a person's life goals."

George Mason University psychologist Todd Kashdan studied over 170 college students who experienced death of loved ones, debilitating accidents, or violence. Those who explored their anxiety (not avoided it) experienced the highest levels of growth.

**Magness's OCD**

Magness suffered from obsessive-compulsive disorder since childhood – believed stepping on a crack would break his mother's back, had to touch doorknobs front and back, turn alarm on/off seven times before bed. His Southern conservative family in the 1990s thought seeing a "shrink" was a sign of weakness. They taught avoidance.

In OCD, thought-action fusion occurs – thinking a terrible thought feels as bad as doing it. Research shows OCD sufferers' brains have difficulty learning what's "safe" – when a green face was associated with electric shock, then the shock was removed, the control group quickly learned safety, but the OCD group couldn't let go of the lingering threat (prefrontal cortex wasn't firing).

Magness learned to create space between thought and action. "Those who society sees as weak often are the strongest on the inside."

**Conclusion**

Real toughness is acceptance: of who you are, what you're going through, and the discomfort that comes with it. Biographer Joshua Wolf Shenk on Lincoln: "He did not pretend to be anything other than he was." Be who you are. That's real toughness.

## The Basic Categories

Seven primary types: Projects list, Project support material, Calendar actions and information, Next Actions lists, Waiting For list, Reference material, Someday/Maybe list.

**Hard edges are critical.** Categories must be kept visually, physically, and psychologically separate. If reference mixes with "to read" items, you go numb to the stack. If Next Actions that belong on the calendar stay on action lists, you won't trust your calendar. If inactive projects stay on Projects list instead of Someday/Maybe, you lose rigorous action-generating focus.

**All you need are lists and folders.** Lists can be: (1) a file folder with separate paper notes, (2) an actual list on titled paper, or (3) an inventory in software. Don't impose external priority scaffolding requiring rearrangement as things change—prioritize intuitively against the whole list.

## Organizing Action Reminders

After processing "in," you'll have 20–70+ pending items. Sort into meaningful groupings.

**Calendar actions** are time-specific ("10:00–11:00 meet with Jim") or day-specific ("Call Rachel Tuesday"). The calendar should show only the "hard landscape"—commitments you absolutely must do that day. Resist putting actions you'd like to get done but might move.

**As-soon-as-possible actions** are best organized by context (tool, location, or situation). How discrete categories need to be depends on (1) how many actions you track and (2) how often you change contexts. With 25 actions, one list might suffice; with 50–100, you need sorting.

Common list headings:
- **Calls** – all phone calls; record phone numbers alongside each item. A discrete Calls category makes it easier to focus and intuitively pick the best call.
- **At Computer** – actions requiring a computer. If you fly without Wi-Fi, maintain a separate Online list. If mobile-centric, a single Digital context list or Anywhere category might work best.
- **Errands** – out-and-about tasks. Track sublists within items (e.g., "hardware store" with appended items). Location-based reminders from mobile devices are a nice option but overoptimistic for keeping your head clear without a rigorously managed list.
- **At Office** – actions requiring physical presence at the office. With "hotel-ing" on the rise, you may need separate At Office "A" and "B" lists for different locations.
- **At Home** – home-only actions. If you work only at home, the At Home list can suffice.
- **Agendas** – items to cover with specific people or in standing meetings. Keep separate lists for bosses, partners, assistants, children, attorneys, etc. Your system should allow you to add Agendas ad hoc, as needed quickly and simply.
- **Read/Review** – longer-than-two-minute reading items, best managed in a separate physical stack tray. Some professionals also use a Review/Respond category for more rigorous reading. For digital input, a Review/Watch folder or Surf Web action list can hold links to videos, blogs, or online articles.

**Waiting For** – reminders of deliverables from others (e.g., tickets ordered, scanner coming, proposal approval). Include the date requested and any agreed-upon due date. Review as often as needed to assess whether to check status. Keep this list close at hand, in the same system as your Next Actions lists, because responsibility for the next step may bounce back and forth many times before a project is finished.

**Using original items as reminders** – efficient for Read/Review materials (e.g., magazine in tray) and for bills in a "Bills to Pay" folder. For e-mail, create @ACTION and @WAITING FOR folders that sort to the top of your navigator bar. Verifiable to some degree, but still rely on faith because some things are impossible to test (e.g., money's intrinsic value, national citizenship) and because humans generalize from little evidence. Bad ideologies (racism, sexism) persist due to ignorance more than malice.
3. **Interpersonal religions** (other people, e.g., romantic love, sports heroes, celebrities, politics). "Easy" mode—common as people themselves. ## The Formula of Humanity

### How to Grow Up

Psychological development proceeds through stages of value formation. Young children are driven by exploration, building a value hierarchy from pleasure and pain (e.g., ice cream is good, hot stoves are bad). This is the Feeling Brain collecting information on what to pursue or avoid. The child’s identity is small and fragile, constituted by immediate pleasure and pain—Susie likes chocolate, is afraid of dogs, enjoys coloring, is mean to her brother. The child cannot yet conceive of others’ perspectives; they are like little tyrants.

Adolescence begins when the child recognizes the world is too vast to explore fully. The two brains shift from trying everything to developing abstract rules (e.g., all flames are dangerous, stealing always upsets Mom). Witold Pilecki, a decorated Polish-Soviet War officer, voluntarily entered Auschwitz in 1940 to organize a resistance and mutiny. ### The Uncomfortable Truth

The Uncomfortable Truth: "One day, you and everyone you love will die. And beyond a small group of people for an extremely brief period of time, little of what you say or do will ever matter." Everything we think or do is an elaborate avoidance of this. We are "inconsequential cosmic dust" on a tiny blue speck. The universe does not care about our concerns. We care, and we project imagined importance onto the world to avoid being crushed by our material insignificance.

### Hope as a Psychological Necessity

Hope is the fuel for our mental engine. Without hope, we spiritually die. The opposite of happiness is not anger or sadness—those mean you still give a fuck. Chronic anxiety is a crisis of hope (fear of a failed future). Depression is a crisis of hope (belief in a meaningless future). Delusion, addiction, and obsession are the mind's desperate attempts to generate hope.

Religious people suffer from depression and commit suicide in far fewer numbers than nonreligious people because practiced faith protects them from the Uncomfortable Truth.

### The Paradox of Progress

Materially, things are better than ever, yet we seem to be losing our minds. This is the paradox of progress: the better things get, the more anxious and desperate we feel. Writers like Steven Pinker and Hans Rosling argue things are the best they've ever been: people are more educated, violence is down, racism and sexism are at historic lows, extreme poverty is at an all-time low, wars are smaller and less frequent, children die less, people live longer, and there's more wealth. Our minds construct "hope narratives"—before/after stories—to maintain hope. When the author's grandfather died, he felt he must live to make him proud, even though it was irrational (his grandfather was dead, they weren't close). This is a common feeling. These narratives give life purpose: they imply something better in the future and that it's achievable. Finding one's "life's purpose" means figuring out what to hope for. Religious people suffer from depression and commit suicide in far fewer numbers than nonreligious people because practiced faith protects them from the Uncomfortable Truth.

### The Paradox of Progress

Materially, things are better than ever, yet we seem to be losing our minds. This is the paradox of progress: the better things get, the more anxious and desperate we feel. Writers like Steven Pinker and Hans Rosling argue things are the best they've ever been: people are more educated, violence is down, racism and sexism are at historic lows, extreme poverty is at an all-time low, wars are smaller and less frequent, children die less, people live longer, and there's more wealth. But these are statistics about the past, not the future. Hope is based on visions of the future.

Despite progress, in the U.S., depression and anxiety are on an 80-year upswing among young people and a 20-year upswing among adults. Since 1985, life satisfaction has declined. Stress levels have risen over 30 years. Drug overdoses hit an all-time high with the opioid crisis. Nearly half of all Americans report feeling isolated. Social trust is plummeting. In the 1980s, the most common answer for "how many people have you discussed important personal matters with in the last six months" was "three"; by 2006, it was "zero." The environment is "completely fucked." Extremism, conspiracy theories, and survivalist subcultures are growing. The wealthier and safer the place you live, the more likely you are to commit suicide.

Hope doesn't care about solved problems. It cares only about problems that still need to be solved. The better the world gets, the more we have to lose, and the less we feel we have to hope for.

### Three Components of Hope

To build and maintain hope, we need three things: (1) a sense of control (we can affect our fate), (2) a belief in the value of something (something worth striving for), and (3) a community (a group that values the same things). Lose any of the three, and you lose hope. The next three chapters examine these areas: control (chapter 2), values (chapter 3), and communities (chapter 4).

## The Junction Boys Myth

In 1954, Texas A&M coach Paul "Bear" Bryant took nearly 100 players to Junction, Texas, for a brutal preseason camp designed to "separate the quitters from the keepers." After ten days of scrimmaging in a drought and heat wave, only 27–35 remained. The camp is memorialized as a toughness blueprint—but the team went 1–9 that season. The undefeated 1956 team relied on freshmen who hadn't attended Junction (including Heisman winner John David Crow) and blue-chip recruits acquired partly through rule-breaking. Survivors like Jack Pardee stayed because they had no other choice, not innate toughness. Bryant later apologized, admitting "if it had been me, I'd have quit a dozen times."

## The Military's Real Lesson

The military doesn't use boot camps to *develop* toughness—it uses them to *sort*. The actual development model is stress inoculation, exemplified by the SERE program. SERE has three phases: classroom (teaching skills like psychology, camouflage, fire-making), evasion (wilderness survival), and detention (simulated POW captivity). The classroom phase is critical—without learning coping skills first, the harrowing phases are useless. As sports psychologist Brian Zuleger put it, "Telling people to relax doesn't work unless you've taught people how to actually relax."

Research shows 96% of soldiers experience dissociative symptoms under extreme stress; 65% "lost track of what was going on." The military now emphasizes building a "mental skills foundation"—confidence, goal setting, attention control, imagery, self-talk—before exposure to stress. Programs like Comprehensive Soldier Fitness (CSF) and the Army's Human Dimension Strategy focus on holistic development, not sorting.

## The Inner Battle and the Path to Toughness

Toughness isn't bulldozing through discomfort. High performers all want to quit under extreme stress—negative thoughts are normal, representing the mind's attempt to protect us. The key is navigating the sequence: **Feel → Inner debate → Urge → Decision** (freak out or find a way through). The brain is an uncertainty-reducing machine; it seeks closure. Toughness means creating space between unease and the quickest solution, training the mind to handle uncertainty long enough to choose the correct response, not the easiest one.

Soldiers who keep a clear head under stress: (1) appraise stress as a challenge, not a threat; (2) use diverse coping methods (cognitive flexibility); (3) process internal signals without reacting; (4) change their physiological state rather than reacting to negative stimuli.

## The Aggregation of Marginal Gains

In 2003, British Cycling hired Dave Brailsford. British riders had won one Olympic gold since 1908 and no Tour de France in 110 years. One manufacturer refused to sell bikes, fearing it would hurt sales if pros saw the Brits using their gear.

Brailsford implemented "the aggregation of marginal gains": searching for a tiny margin of improvement in everything. He said, "if you broke down everything you could think of that goes into riding a bike, and then improve it by 1 percent, you will get a significant increase when you put them all together."

Changes included redesigning seats, rubbing alcohol on tires, electrically heated overshorts, biofeedback sensors, wind-tunnel fabric testing, lighter indoor racing suits, testing massage gels, hiring a surgeon to teach hand-washing, determining optimal pillows and mattresses per rider, and painting the team truck white to spot dust.

Five years later, at the 2008 Beijing Olympics, British Cycling won 60% of gold medals. At the 2012 London Olympics, they set nine Olympic and seven world records. Bradley Wiggins became the first British Tour de France winner in 2012; Chris Froome won in 2013, 2015, 2016, and 2017. From 2007 to 2017, British cyclists won 178 world championships and 66 Olympic or Paralympic gold medals.

## Why Small Habits Make a Big Difference

Improving by 1% per day for one year makes you 37 times better. Getting 1% worse per day declines nearly to zero. Habits are the compound interest of self-improvement. The impact of a small change is like shifting an airplane's heading by 3.5 degrees: from Los Angeles to New York, you land in Washington, D.C.

Outcomes are lagging measures of habits. Net worth lags financial habits; weight lags eating habits; knowledge lags learning habits. Time magnifies the margin between success and failure. Habits are a double-edged sword.

## The Plateau of Latent Potential

Breakthrough moments result from many previous actions building potential. Cancer spends 80% of its life undetectable. Bamboo builds root systems for five years before exploding 90 feet in six weeks. In early stages, there is often a Valley of Disappointment where changes seem ineffective. The most powerful outcomes are delayed. Complaining about not achieving success despite hard work is like complaining an ice cube didn't melt when heated from 25 to 31 degrees. All action happens at 32 degrees. The San Antonio Spurs have a quote from Jacob Riis: "When nothing seems to help, I go and look at a stonecutter hammering away at his rock... Yet at the hundred and first blow it will split in two, and I know it was not that last blow that did it—but all that had gone before."

## Forget Goals, Focus on Systems

Goals are about results you want to achieve. Systems are about the processes that lead to those results. Four problems with goals:
1. Winners and losers have the same goals. Every Olympian wants gold; every candidate wants the job. The goal cannot differentiate winners from losers.
2. Achieving a goal is only a momentary change. Clean a messy room once, but without changing the system, it gets messy again.
3. Goals restrict happiness: "Once I reach my goal, then I'll be happy." They create an either-or conflict.
4. Goals create a yo-yo effect. Many runners stop training after crossing the finish line. The purpose of building systems is to continue playing the game.

"You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems." Atomic habits are tiny changes that are part of a larger system. Just as atoms are building blocks of molecules, atomic habits are building blocks of remarkable results.
